paras: The attempted lynching of William Holmes took place on the night of Sunday, August 6, 1882, when a mob of about a hundred men surrounded the jail at Pomeroy, Ohio, to seize Holmes, a Black man charged with outraging a young white girl near Rutland. The men nearly broke through the jail walls before learning that Holmes had already been taken away and sent to Columbus for safekeeping. The case drew further notice when two alleged leaders of the mob, both of Middleport, were arrested and jailed, and their friends threatened to free them by force.

According to a Pomeroy Journal special carried from Columbus, Holmes, described as "a burly negro," was out hunting on Saturday evening near Rutland when he came on several young white girls picking blackberries. The dispatch charged that he scared off the younger girls and assaulted the eldest, named in different papers as Hysell, Isabel, Isabelle or Hupsell. Neighbors scoured the woods with shotguns, "with a determination to lynch him if found," but officers caught Holmes and placed him in the Pomeroy jail. Some dispatches added that "Holmes has a bad reputation" and that "it is believed he will be lynched yet."

On the night of Sunday, August 6, a mob of about a hundred men surrounded the jail to get Holmes. When they had nearly broken through the walls, they found that he had already been taken away, and he was sent on to Columbus on August 7. The Pomeroy wire stressed that the mob was made up of well-known men who made no effort to conceal their identity. No injuries were reported.

A Pomeroy dispatch of August 10 said the attempt "was conducted so openly" that the authorities had to arrest some of the leaders. W. T. Campbell, local editor of the Middleport Republican, and William Swisher, a saloon keeper, both of Middleport, were brought before a justice for participating in a mob, refused to give bail and were jailed. Their friends declared they would mob the jail to free them, feeling ran high in Middleport and Rutland against the authorities, and the sheriff armed twenty-five men to guard the jail.

The Jackson Standard later reported that the expected rescue never came and that the two men were released on their own recognizance. No report of an indictment or trial of Holmes, or of further proceedings against the mob, appears in the coverage.

The story ran as brief telegraph items in papers from Washington and Memphis to St. Paul, Sacramento, Salt Lake City, Cheyenne, Seattle and Las Vegas, New Mexico, between August 7 and August 19. The first dispatches treated the accusation as fact, under headlines such as "A Negro's Brutal Lust" in the St. Paul Daily Globe and "Brutal Rape" in the Memphis Daily Appeal. The siege itself was headed "Attempted Lynching" in the Las Vegas Daily Gazette and "More About the Rutland Outrage" in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union.

Coverage of the arrests took a more critical tone toward the mob: the Salt Lake Herald headed its item "Pseudo Martyrs," and the West Virginia Freeman ran it as "Would be Lynchers in Jail," saying the participants were "now paying for their lawlessness." The nearby Jackson Standard called the mob "both awkward and cowardly" and described the charge as only an attempt.

Accounts differ on dates: early dispatches put the alleged assault on Saturday, August 5, while others say "last evening" or "Sabbath evening," and several briefs put the siege "at midnight on Monday" rather than Sunday night. The first reports described a completed assault on the eldest of several girls, whereas the Jackson Standard and an Owosso paper described an attempted assault, the former on a girl out with her mother. One Seattle dispatch called the prisoner George Holmes, and the second arrested man's name varies with the printing.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of William Holmes
bases: A crowd of about a hundred men tried to break into the Pomeroy jail to lynch a Black prisoner accused of assaulting a white girl, after armed neighbors had searched the woods for him (A1, A3, A25).

Holmes had been removed to Columbus before the mob nearly broke through the jail walls, so no one was killed; the papers describe an attempted lynching by about a hundred men acting on a rape accusation (A3, A7, A25).
Several wire dispatches, a Pomeroy Journal special and an independent Ohio account in the Jackson Standard agree on the accusation, the jail siege and the removal to Columbus (A3, A21, A25, A35).

record_check.dossier: Aug. 5 is the reported date of the alleged assault and possibly the woods search; the jail siege was Sunday night, Aug. 6 (into Aug. 7).
One person, William ('Bill') Holmes; the duplicate 'Holmes' entry should be merged. One dispatch says George.
No seizure by the mob: officers caught and jailed Holmes and removed him before the siege. Armed search (pursuit), armed gathering and jail siege are supported.
About a hundred well-known men; W. T. Campbell (Middleport Republican) and William Swisher (saloon keeper), of Middleport, were arrested as leaders.
A mob of private citizens (armed neighbors, then a jail mob), not a posse.

William (Wm., 'Bill') Holmes, described as 'a burly negro'; one dispatch calls him George Holmes
Charged with outraging a young white girl (named Hysell, Isabel, or Hupsell) while she was blackberrying near Rutland; later accounts say an attempt
Well-known men who made no effort to conceal themselves; two alleged leaders were W. T. Campbell, local editor of the Middleport Republican, and William Swisher, a saloon keeper, both of Middleport
